extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and students assembling photographs, slides, and illustrations for press releases and PR presentations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, producing, formatting, supplying, evaluating, and presenting photographs, slides, and illustrations as part of public relations materials (press releases, photo essays, slide shows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a communication objective for each photograph
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t choose a photo just because it is interesting or artistic; determine what message you intend to communicate with the photo and whether the person who sees the photo will understand and retain that message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The communication objectives that apply to written or spoken messages apply to photographs as well—photographs carry an intended meaning and should be chosen to serve an objective rather than solely for aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage expectations: photos rarely change attitudes or behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to change attitudes or behaviors with photographs alone, so don’t expect those effects very often—although a particularly dramatic photo sometimes may change an attitude or stimulate a behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using photographs to gain attention and interest rather than relying on them to produce major persuasive or behavioral outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider visual complexity relative to publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs are more complex than illustrations, graphs, or similar graphics—they carry more information and viewers can take more varied meanings from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use photographs to gain and hold attention for low-involvement, passive publics; use simpler illustrations or graphs for communicating difficult or technical information to active, high-involvement audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match visual form to information difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Because photographs can carry extraneous information, they are not as useful for communicating difficult ideas—illustrations or graphs may be preferable for financial or technical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience needs clarity and uniform interpretation (e.g., scientists reading a graph), prefer less complex graphic forms that convey the same message consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate photos as part of readership studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask if people remember seeing a photograph to measure exposure; ask what message they think a photograph conveyed to measure message retention; ask whether people believe the photograph portrayed a situation accurately to measure message acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If choosing attitude or behavior objectives, apply attitude/behavior measures from broader research, but recognize it’s extremely difficult to separate effects of photos from accompanying written messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure media-placement effect of photos
rubrics_metrics.description: When you send pictures with press releases, compare press clippings to see success in getting on the media agenda when a picture accompanies a release versus when it goes out alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clipping analysis to assess whether including a photo increases media pickup or prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget photography costs before choosing source
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs vary greatly—from taking photos in-house (time, film, processing) to hiring expensive freelance photographers (top-flight photographers may charge $1,000 for a single photograph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider frequency of need and cost-per-shot; an in-house photographer can pay off if volume is high; plan set-up costs for darkrooms or equipment accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize photographic assets with numbering/cataloging
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute a numbering and cataloging system so every single picture has its own identification and can be found in the proper place (e.g., roll-year-set-frame codes like 84-24-15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place negatives in plastic holders, make contact sheets, serially stamp contact strips, and record frame numbers on prints to track thousands of pictures efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply media-standard photo sizes and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred size for submissions to newspapers and magazines using black-and-white photos is 8-by-10 inches; 5-by-7 is sufficient for head-and-shoulders; 4-by-5 used by some to save budget; 35-mm color transparency is most common for magazines using color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sizes that editors can reduce rather than enlarge to ensure better engraving quality; offer horizontal and vertical versions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide appropriate finish for medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Photos for print should be glossy; for television provide a matte-finish print that will not reflect into the television lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For glossy finish dry a photo against smooth metal; for matte press it against woven cloth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide camera-ready halftones to increase pickup
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering camera-ready halftone reproductions already cropped to standard two- and three-column widths can make editors more likely to use material because it can be pasted right onto layouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although more expensive (printer makes halftone and reproduces multiple slick-paper copies), it can increase chances of placement especially with low-engravings-budget outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and attach cutline information correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutline information is typed double-spaced, duplicated on white paper; glue or tape a one-inch fold of the sheet to the back of the photograph and fold remainder to protect the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both short cutlines (few words describing action when accompanying a release) and longer stand-alone cutlines (all pertinent news information) because you can’t always know how an editor will use the photo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume photographer credit or usage releases
rubrics_metrics.description: PR photos do not normally carry a credit line unless agreed with a known artist; it is assumed that permission has been granted by identifiable persons to use their likenesses, and failure to obtain permissions can negate PR value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain legal releases from identifiable persons to avoid later complications (see legal constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail and deliver photos to protect them
rubrics_metrics.description: Mail photographs in manila envelopes with a cardboard liner and a 'Photo Do Not Fold' warning; consider hand-delivery/courier because media often do not return unused photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use protective packaging to avoid scratches or soiling; expect that media may file unused photos in a library rather than return them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects that show context and avoid staged clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Walk through locations to find subjects that will make dramatic or storytelling shots; show subject in context, naturally, and avoid the standard head-and-shoulders mug shot and staged poses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of ways to avoid stock poses (person at desk on phone, group of retirees in semicircle, one person handing a check, speaker at podium with potted palm), and instruct photographers to aim for candid moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose images that summarize the idea and have human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting from contact sheets, seek the single photograph that summarizes the idea, with the most human interest or emotional appeal (close-up of a face, gesture), then supporting shots for multipicture spreads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also check tonal quality, focus, and contrast for consistent excellence across selected images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoot many frames to capture candid moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Press photographers shoot dozens—even scores—of pictures in quick succession to capture the moment when the guard is down and the subject appears 'real.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique helps avoid the posed look of executives or habitual 'camera-aware' subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crop photos purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Crop to highlight a specific object or detail, reduce ambiguity or remove distractions, fit a juxtaposition/scheme, or bring shapes/directions into consonance with external elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cropping can eliminate repetitive elements, redirect the viewer's eye, keep subject size consistent across adjacent photos, or align picture shapes with page layout; use contact sheets with grease-pen marks or simple cardboard cornices to plan crops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distracting or ambiguous elements when cropping
rubrics_metrics.description: Details that enhance a single photo may be extraneous when used with other shots (e.g., a hand pointing into an adjacent picture), so the editor may chop the person off at mid-torso or otherwise crop to remove distractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check how a cropped image will interact with adjacent images and type on the layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size photos correctly for reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how much a shot must be reduced or enlarged for engraving—editors work with standard column widths and order pictures two or three columns wide with depth variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate reproduction dimensions by proportion (algebraic ratio), or use proportioning wheel, Scaleograph, or simple ruler/light-table technique (draw diagonal and measure to find reproduced depth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use crop marks and simple tools to estimate final composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Crop marks may be made on contact sheets or glossy prints with grease pencil; use L-shaped cardboard cornices or paper to frame and visualize crops before marking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any two sheets of paper can be used for quick cropping; practical tools simplify planning prior to enlargement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry-mount prints intended for display
rubrics_metrics.description: Prints intended for display should be dry mounted (laminated to stiff backing) to stay flat and prevent buckling, creasing, bubbling, or other imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mounting presses, mounting board, dry-glue tissues, tacking iron, and paper cutter are basic supplies; small operations can often access press use at supply houses; store mounted pictures in envelopes until display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan photo story layout with anchor and supporting shots
rubrics_metrics.description: Group individual pictures so they make a statement greater than the sum of parts: include an all-purpose anchor picture, emotional human-interest shots, steps leading to culmination, context-setting and reaction shots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank shots by visual effect and storytelling ability; the anchor picture should be placed so the viewer begins and ends with it and is usually twice as large as other photos; the essay must have a beginning and end to achieve PR objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate sources for illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: When illustrations rather than photos are needed, sources include clip-art services (simple line drawings), computer-generated graphics (pie-charts, bar graphs), and staff or freelance artists who produce illustrations to order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clip-art can be pasted onto camera-ready layouts without engraving; computer graphics allow labeling and dimension control; cultivate an artist who understands your publication's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match slide-show objectives to PR model and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Slide shows can be used in all four PR models but with different intent: press agents use them to promote products/events; public-information specialists to disseminate information; two-way asymmetric for persuasion/emotion; two-way symmetric as a preliminary position and discussion trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the communicator’s intent up front because it affects content, tone, and whether a slide show is appropriate at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use slide shows to supplement face-to-face contact and specific PR programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Slide shows are useful only when group sessions with target publics are set up—common uses include community relations, employee relations, financial relations, promotion/fund raising, and educational relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy reliance on slides for press presentations (reporters prefer dialogue) and avoid filling dialogue sessions with slides for activist publics who want to argue and discuss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have objectives, know your publics, and pretest slide shows
rubrics_metrics.description: As with photos, have an objective and effect in mind for the slide show; ask what the audience already knows and what you want it to know; maximize message retention and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretest on a sample audience using questionnaires similar to chapter-9 measures or signaled stopping technique (list slides and have viewers indicate where they'd stop for confusion/agreement/understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive complexity in multimedia presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex multimedia presentations can arouse interest and emotions but may not communicate a clear message; if you want a clear message to come across, don’t make the presentation too complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance visual complexity with clarity of message; sequencing can increase involvement but may sacrifice message clarity if overly intricate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget slide-show costs and consider renting vs buying
rubrics_metrics.description: Slide shows can cost little (labor, film, processing) or be expensive with sophisticated equipment and personnel; evaluate how often you'll present before investing in equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider renting equipment or contracting outside specialists; use Gantt charts and network analyses for planning; weigh costs against frequency of use to captive audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and script presentations before selecting visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the major points of the presentation (content) before worrying about exact visuals—start with message/points so objectives are explicit and not subordinated to pleasing visuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break outline into (1) individual pieces of information and (2) visual images that will illustrate those concepts; use a split script with concepts on one side and visuals on the other; write narration after visuals are decided and choose live vs recorded narration and narrator type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure synchronization and sufficiency of visuals and narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Once script and visuals are decided, check if more shots are needed; condense visuals where narration is insufficient to cover slide sequences to prevent 'stalling' in sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about live versus recorded narration affect coordination; recorded narration ensures accuracy and timing; plan shot length to match narration.
